title: JPMorgan outlines how the S&P 500 can soar more than 20% in the next year - Yahoo Finance
text: JPMorgan outlines how the S&P 500 can soar more than 20% in the next year Jennifer Sor May 22, 2026 3 min read ^GSPC OP-USD JPMorgan Private Bank thinks the S&P 500 could soar 22% in the next year in its bull case for stocks. The bank said the rally was possible if AI produced large productivity gains that kept a lid on inflation. Stocks will likely tolerate higher bond yields if growth expectations are strong, they added. 9,000 could be the new number to watch for the S&P 500 . JPMorgan Private Bank said that it sees a path for the benchmark index to smash through 9,000 over the next year, implying a 22% rally from current levels. Despite broader concerns about inflation and the Iran war , there's a chance the market's general uptrend could continue, assuming that the AI supercycle ends up being larger than markets previously thought, Kriti Gupta, a global investment strategist, and Nick Roberts, a portfolio manager at JPMorgan Private Bank, wrote in a note on Wednesday. "While not the base case, the S&P 500 could reach as high as 9,000 by mid-2027. A ~22% gain from current levels may seem optimistic, but it remains entirely plausible," Gupta and Roberts said. The bank pointed to how the tech sector is on another tear this year, largely due to strong earnings and continued optimism about AI. Technology stocks in the S&P 500 are up 23% year-to-date, outpacing the 8% increase in the broader index. Some investors are concerned that gains in the market are overly concentrated in tech, but the rally also offers an "opportunity," the bank said, assuming that AI helps accelerate productivity . If workers are more productive, corporate earnings could still grow at more than 10% rate without stoking inflation, the bank speculated, a key constraint analysts have warned could hold the AI trade back. "We've seen it before. Productivity boomed in the late 1990s, annualizing ~2.8%. Meanwhile, the index delivered five consecutive years of over 20% returns between 1995 and 2000. It can happen again," the firm wrote. The outlook for markets is still mostly upbeat, though it's grown somewhat cloudier as the Iran war continues and the economy starts to feel the effects. The primary fear is that inflation could spiral, fueled by higher energy prices which leak into other consumer goods. That, in turn, could lead to higher-for-longer rates and weigh on risk assets like stocks. Concern about the outlook for stocks grew this week amid a historic sell-off in government bonds , with investors dumping US Treasurys amid anxiety about inflation. But the recent moves in yields — such a 40 basis-point jump in the 10-year US Treasury — "isn't uncommon," Gupta and Roberts said, citing previous episodes when bond yields large but short-lived spike. Story Continues Stocks will likely be able to tolerate higher yields if the market has higher growth expectations for the economy, they added. "Risk assets do not always go up in a straight line. The current unwind in momentum stocks like semiconductors and other AI bottleneck trades in reaction to higher bond yields is entirely healthy. It sets the stage for the next leg up, with cleaner investor positioning," Gupta and Roberts said. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.
